text: This is what a woman looks like when she's about to get married. And this is what a man looks like when he's about to get married. Do you see any difference? Well, actually, the father walking the bride down the aisle to the groom is symbolic of passing down the ownership of the bride from the father to the groom. And that is a tradition we still see nowadays that was kept from when there was an over-patriarchy governing society. It used to represent the passage of ownership, protection, and care of the bride from the father to the groom. So why are we still doing this? Disgusting. So, is she right that a father walking his daughter down the aisle represents one man transferring ownership of her to another? Partly, but ownership is the strongest and most simplistic version of a much more complicated history. The tradition absolutely developed in societies where women lived under extensive male authority. In England, the 1549 Book of Common Prayer instructed the minister to ask, who gives this woman to be married to this man? The minister would then receive the woman from her father's or friend's hands and place her hand in the groom's. And under English curvature, marriage severely restricted a woman's independent legal identity. A married woman generally could not own property, enter contracts, or control her earnings in the same way as an unmarried woman. So the ceremony could symbolize her moving from her father's household and protection into her husband's. That is genuinely patriarchal history. Women were subjected to male guardianship and control, but they were not legally identical to property that could simply be owned and sold. Medieval church law also recognized the consent of both spouses as what created a valid marriage. A father could apply a normal social pressure and families regularly arranged marriages, but his decision alone was not supposed to create a valid Christian marriage without the couple's consent. Even that old 1549 ceremony said the bride could be presented by her father or a friend. It was not exclusively about a father handing his property to another man. She's also treating one particular Anglo-American wedding arrangement as if it were universal. In Jewish weddings, both the bride and groom are commonly escorted by their parents. In many Catholic ceremonies, the couple may enter together or both may be accompanied. So the lonely groom waiting at the front is not simply what men look like when they are getting married. It is one cultural way of staging a wedding. And most importantly, the historical origin of a tradition does not automatically determine what it means today. A father accompanying his adult daughter can now symbolize love, emotional support, or the importance of their relationship. He is not signing over the title deed to a human being. If a bride dislikes the historical symbolism, she can walk alone with both parents or together with her partner. But calling a modern family gesture disgusting because of one interpretation of its historical roots ignores how traditions change and how the people participating in them actually understand them.
